query: For magnetic high-entropy alloys, what single intervention could increase the coercive field? State one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the mechanism expected to alter coercivity, the predicted outcome relative to a matched baseline, the conditions under which the effect should hold, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Rapid thermal annealing (RTA) of disordered HEA thin films induces chemical ordering that increases coercivity by enhancing magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
generation.material_initial_state: Magnetically soft, disordered high-entropy alloy thin films (e.g., FeCoNiMnCu) deposited at room temperature with low coercivity.
generation.intervention: Subject the as-deposited HEA films to a rapid thermal annealing process (e.g., ~15 seconds at a target temperature optimized for the alloy, such as 700–800 °C) under controlled ambient conditions.
generation.conditions: Films are deposited on thermally oxidized substrates and annealed in a controlled atmosphere (e.g., inert or vacuum environment) to promote substrate-induced strain and chemical ordering while avoiding dewetting or excessive grain growth.
generation.structural_mediator: Transformation from a disordered solid solution to a chemically ordered phase (e.g., L1₀ or similar) accompanied by structural distortions that enhance anisotropy.
generation.mechanism: The RTA-induced chemical ordering elevates the magnetocrystalline anisotropy by creating an ordered arrangement of constituent elements, which increases the energy barrier for domain wall movement, thereby significantly enhancing the coercive field.
generation.predicted_outcome: RTA-treated films will exhibit a marked (up to 40-fold or more) increase in coercivity relative to as-deposited films, with XRD and TEM confirming the emergence of the ordered phase.
generation.baseline: As-deposited, disordered HEA thin films with low coercivity (approximately 10 Oe) and no chemical order.
generation.boundary: The effect is dependent on film thickness, substrate type, and finely tuned RTA parameters; over-annealing may lead to undesired morphological changes such as dewetting or excessive grain growth.
generation.uncertainty: The precise coercivity enhancement and phase purity depend on optimizing processing parameters, which requires systematic study across different HEA compositions. (Although variations in parameters exist, prior studies support the effectiveness of RTA in enhancing coercivity through ordering.)

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical sets of HEA thin films, anneal one set using the specified rapid thermal annealing parameters, and leave the other set as-deposited. Use high-resolution XRD and TEM to confirm the emergence of chemical ordering, and perform magnetic hysteresis measurements (via SQUID/VSM) to assess changes in coercivity.
measurements: XRD (including reciprocal space mapping) to detect ordered phase formation
TEM for microstructural confirmation of chemical ordering
Magnetic hysteresis loops for coercivity and anisotropy evaluation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If RTA-treated films do not show statistically significant increases in coercivity and there is no evidence of chemical ordering relative to as-deposited films, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe vast high entropy alloy (HEA) composition space is promising for discovery of new material phases with unique properties. This study explores the potential to achieve rare‐earth‐free high magnetic anisotropy materials in single‐phase HEA thin films. Thin films of FeCoNiMnCu sputtered on thermally oxidized Si/SiO2 substrates at room temperature are magnetically soft, with a coercivity on the order of 10 Oe. After post‐deposition rapid thermal annealing (RTA), the films exhibit a single face‐centered‐cubic phase, with an almost 40‐fold increase in coercivity. Inclusion of 50 at.% Pt in the film leads to ordering of a single L10 high entropy intermetallic phase after RTA, along with high magnetic anisotropy and 3 orders of magnitude coercivity increase. These results demonstrate a promising HEA approach to achieve high magnetic anisotropy materials using RTA.Keywords: high entropy alloy, magnetic anisotropy, rapid thermal annealing High entropy alloy (HEA) thin films are explored to achieve high magnetic anisotropy phases. Certain HEA compositions may exhibit long‐range chemical order through the emergence of multiple sublattices, analogous to high entropy ceramics,[  ] leading to so‐called “high entropy intermetallic” (HEI) compounds.[  ] Previously, transition metal alloys with high anisotropy, such as the L10 phases of FePt and FePd have been achieved by annealing of equiatomic solid solution pre‐cursors.[  ] In the case of metastable high anisotropy phases such as L10 FeNi, unconventional annealing techniques have been employed.[  ] In particular, rapid thermal annealing (RTA) of transition metal alloy films on Si/SiO2 is an effective means of inducing high anisotropy phase formation in solid solution precursors, in part due to the substrate‐induced strain.[  ] In this study, we experimentally demonstrate two thin film HEAs with large coercivity and magnetic anisotropy achieved by RTA. We show that RTA treatment of equiatomic FeCoNiMnCu thin films leads to ≈40‐fold increase in coercivity. By introduction of 50 at.% Pt, we realize an L10 HEI phase of (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy resulting from a reduced lattice symmetry and strong spin‐orbit coupling.
